title: Lay and monastic
hookLine: some schools center the monastery, others the household

lines: DAWN IN LAOS: THE ALMS ROUND.
cards: First light, a quiet street in Laos. A line of monks in orange robes walks barefoot, bowls held in front of them. Along the curb, people kneel on mats with baskets of sticky rice still warm from the steamer.
A pinch of rice into each bowl. No one speaks. The monks don't ask.
At the end, a short chant of blessing from the monks to the people who gave. Two kinds of life, meeting on one sidewalk at dawn, each feeding the other.

teach.b: First, the monastery at the center. In Theravada lands, the sangha of monks and nuns keeps the full discipline, studies and meditates, and depends on lay people for food, robes and medicine.
In return, monks give the teaching and blessings. It's an exchange, not charity in one direction. Second, the householder in the old texts.

The Pali canon honors lay disciples by name: Anathapindika, the merchant who bought a park to give to the Buddha; Visakha, the generous laywoman; and Citta, a householder so learned that, in one discourse, he explains a fine point of the teaching to monks.
In the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha gives a young householder a whole ethic of family life: parents and children, teachers and students, friends, workers. Third, the household at the center.
In Japan, Shinran, of the Pure Land school, whom you met in year three, married and raised a family, and described himself as neither monk nor layman.
The Jodo Shinshu temples that followed him are often led by married priests and their families. In Tibet, some householder yogis, called ngakpas, keep tantric vows while raising children and farming.

Fourth, the layman who outtalks everyone. In the Vimalakirti Sutra, a wealthy householder falls ill, and the great disciples and bodhisattvas are each reluctant to visit, because he has bested them all in debate.
When the question of non-duality finally comes, Vimalakirti answers with silence, and the sutra praises that silence.
Some schools center the monastery, others the household, and each gives its reasons.

how: In Theravada countries lay people offer food to monks on the morning alms round and receive teaching and blessings in return; in Japanese Jodo Shinshu, married priests often lead temples, and householders practice at home.

o: two ranks of monks, the senior and the newly ordained
the rule that only monks may teach and lay people only give
the two lives of the sangha: renouncing a household or living in one

p: a householder who taught monks a point
a layman who answered with silence

s: the alms round is one-way charity
it's an exchange: food, robes and medicine given; teaching and blessings given back.
he was a wealthy householder whom the great disciples were reluctant to visit.
in the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha teaches an ethic of family life
parents and children, teachers and students, friends, workers.

games.q: you're Shinran, a Pure Land monk in Japan. you've come to believe practice belongs in ordinary life too. what do you do?
o: stay in the monastery and keep it to yourself.
marry, raise a family, and keep teaching.
games.why: Shinran married and raised a family, calling himself neither monk nor layman; the temples that followed him are often led by married priests.

practice: Bring to mind someone who gave up a household for a life of practice, a monk, a nun, anyone who chose simplicity, and breathe with gratitude for what their choice keeps alive.
Then bring to mind someone practicing in a busy household, a parent at a stove, a worker on a late shift, and breathe with respect for that too. Let both sit in you together.

wordCard.voice: Lay and monastic. The two lives of the sangha: those who renounce a household for the discipline, and those who practice within one. Schools center them differently, and honor both. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit upasaka: a lay follower (upasika for a woman).

carryVoice: Your line: two lives. Each school honors the other life in its own way. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Shinran, Kyogyoshinsho, postscript ('neither monk nor layman')
